samples.summary: SSRF gate fails open when the DNS pre-resolution errors (or returns nothing)
samples.evidence: `assertFetchableImageUrl` resolves the hostname and, on any rejection from `lookup`, `return`s — i.e. allows the fetch (image-fetcher.ts:203-209). The same happens if the resolver answers with an empty array, since `addresses.some(isPrivateAddress)` is then false (line 210). The gate's own comment frames this as "let the fetch report it", but the gate and the fetch perform two independent resolutions. An attacker who controls the authoritative nameserver for a `src` host (document content is attacker-influenced — anyone who can edit or share the doc picks the `src`) can answer the gate's `getaddrinfo` with SERVFAIL/timeout and then answer undici's connect-time resolution with `169.254.169.254` or `127.0.0.1`, and the CLI will GET it and embed the bytes in the PDF/DOCX/PPTX the victim opens. Any transient resolver hiccup also silently disables the control for that request. Fail-closed (block, classified as a network error) would preserve the diagnosability the comment is after without turning a resolver error into an allow.

samples.summary: isPrivateAddress omits IPv6 transition ranges that embed IPv4 (NAT64 64:ff9b::/96, 6to4 2002::/16, Teredo 2001::/32)
samples.evidence: `isPrivateAddress` handles dotted-quad IPv4, `::`/`::1`, IPv4-mapped/-compatible (`::ffff:*`), `fc00::/7` and `fe80::/10` (lines 131-148), but not the transition prefixes that carry an IPv4 address in later words. On a network with a NAT64 gateway (common on IPv6-only hosts and some CI runners), a `src` of `http://[64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe]/latest/meta-data/` is a literal, passes `ipLiteral`, is not matched by any rule (words[0]=0x0064 → first=0x00, not fc/fd, not fe80), is allowed, and reaches 169.254.169.254. `2002:7f00:1::` (6to4 → 127.0.0.1) is the same shape. Also unmatched on the IPv4 side: 198.18.0.0/15, 192.0.0.0/24, 224.0.0.0/4 and 255.255.255.255. Severity reflects the SSRF impact if the deployment has such a gateway; confidence is low because it depends on the host's network having NAT64/6to4 configured.

samples.summary: Gate resolves the name but the fetch resolves again — DNS rebinding window (acknowledged)
samples.evidence: `assertFetchableImageUrl(target, ...)` at image-fetcher.ts:254 validates the addresses a name currently answers with, then `fetchOrThrow` (line 255) hands the *name* to undici, which resolves it again at connect time. A short-TTL record that answers publicly for the gate's query and with 127.0.0.1 for the connect defeats the check entirely. The code comments (lines 157-160) and the design doc name this as a residual gap, so this is recorded rather than disputed — closing it needs a pinned-address connect (custom undici dispatcher / `lookup` hook), which is feasible but not attempted here.

samples.summary: The configured server origin is a blanket SSRF exemption for every path on that origin
samples.evidence: `if (serverOrigin && url.origin === serverOrigin) return;` (image-fetcher.ts:184) short-circuits every subsequent check. With the documented dev setup `--server http://localhost:3000`, an attacker-authored document can set `src` to any path on that origin — `http://localhost:3000/api/v1/...`, `/actuator`, `/debug` — and the CLI will GET it and embed the response bytes into the exported artifact the victim then reads. Mitigations: no Authorization header or cookies are attached (image-fetcher.ts:225-228), so only unauthenticated internal endpoints are reachable. Narrowing the exemption to the `/images/` path prefix would keep the dev/self-hosted case working without opening the whole origin.

samples.summary: The login nonce — the only binding for the loopback callback — is printed to stderr along with the port
samples.evidence: `console.error(`Opening browser: ${oauthUrl}`)` at login.ts:176 prints `.../auth/github?mode=cli&port=<port>&nonce=<nonce>`, and login.ts:181 passes the same URL to `open` as argv. The nonce is the sole secret binding the `127.0.0.1:<port>/callback` listener (login.ts:299). Anyone who can read that line — a CI job log, a captured terminal transcript, a shared tmux pane, another same-user process reading `ps` — has both the port and the nonce within the 30s window and can drive their own browser through `/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<port>&nonce=<nonce>`, causing the backend to deliver a code for the *attacker's* GitHub account to the victim's listener, which will accept it: account fixation. The task notes acknowledge the argv exposure as out of the nonce's threat model; the stderr print widens it to log files. Printing the URL without the nonce (with the nonce only in the `open` call, or offering to print the full URL only on demand) would keep the fallback usable.

samples.summary: Nonce is still optional in the store type and the controller silently emits a nonce-less loopback redirect
samples.evidence: `CliAuthStore.createState(mode, port, nonce?)` (cli-auth.store.ts:27-31) keeps `nonce` optional, and auth.controller.ts:130-132 degrades silently (`state.nonce ? ... : ''`) rather than refusing. Today the only producer is `GitHubAuthGuard` (github-auth.guard.ts:46), which requires the nonce — so this is not exploitable now. But it leaves the binding as an opt-in property of the caller rather than an invariant of the store: a future or refactored call path that omits the nonce would silently reproduce the pre-nonce behaviour (a code delivered to an arbitrary loopback port that a pre-nonce CLI would accept), and the redirect builder would not object. Making `nonce` required in `createState`/`StateEntry` and throwing in the controller when a `mode === 'cli'` state has none would make the fail-closed property structural.
searchedFor: createState( across packages/backend/src — only github-auth.guard.ts:46 and specs

samples.summary: A remote/local attacker controls which security advice the login timeout prints
samples.evidence: Any unauthenticated request to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=x` (no nonce) sets `sawUnboundCallback = true` (login.ts:300). A hostile web page that guesses the port, or any local process, can therefore force the 30s timeout to print "the server predates nonce-bound CLI login. Upgrade the server" (login.ts:362-365) even when the server is current and the real cause was, say, a closed browser tab. That is attacker-chosen security guidance shown to the operator, and it points them at changing their backend deployment. Distinguishing "a callback arrived that echoed no nonce at all" from "an unrelated request hit the port" is not possible from the request alone, so the message should be phrased as a possibility rather than a diagnosis.

samples.summary: `data:` image URLs return before every other check, with no size or media-type bound
samples.evidence: `if (url.protocol === 'data:') return;` (image-fetcher.ts:174) exits the gate first, and the fetcher then hands the `data:` URL to `fetch`, which materialises the whole payload in memory as a Blob. A document `src` of a multi-hundred-MB `data:` URL is an attacker-controlled memory amplification during export. No network egress is involved, so this is hardening rather than SSRF; a length cap on the `data:` payload before dereferencing would close it.

samples.summary: SystemError keeps the unredacted transport error as `cause` after redacting the message
samples.evidence: errors.ts:165-169 carefully redacts the URL into the message but attaches the original rejection via `{ cause }`. Node's default handler prints `[cause]` (and its message, which for undici can echo the request URL including userinfo/presigned query) for any error that reaches the top level; `bin.ts` installs no top-level handler. Today every `SystemError` is funnelled into `outputError` or `classifyLoginFailure`, which print only `.message`, so I could not complete an exploitable path — hence low confidence. Redacting the cause's message, or omitting `cause`, would remove the footgun.

finding.summary: SSRF gate fails open when the DNS pre-resolution errors (or returns nothing)
finding.evidence: `assertFetchableImageUrl` resolves the hostname and, on any rejection from `lookup`, `return`s — i.e. allows the fetch (image-fetcher.ts:203-209). The same happens if the resolver answers with an empty array, since `addresses.some(isPrivateAddress)` is then false (line 210). verdict.reason: The described fail-open is present verbatim: assertFetchableImageUrl wraps the DNS pre-resolution in a try/catch whose catch arm simply returns (image-fetcher.ts:203-209), allowing the fetch; an empty address array likewise makes addresses.some(isPrivateAddress) false (:210) and falls through to the implicit allow at :215. No compensating guard exists downstream: createImageFetcher calls the gate at :254 and hands the URL to fetchOrThrow (:255-259), which does only `new URL(url)` validation then impl(url, init) (errors.ts:147-171) with no pinned dispatcher and no connect-time private-address check — so the gate and the fetch perform two independent resolutions exactly as the reviewer claims. The repo's own comments establish the threat model (document src is attacker-influenced, :50-54; the gate exists to stop 169.254.169.254 / file-internal fetches being embedded in the exported PDF/DOCX/PPTX, :150-160) and acknowledge only the narrower rebinding gap, not resolver-error fail-open. SSRF is explicitly in the Security lane and this is a weakened control on the enforced path, so major severity stands. No not-present, already-guarded, or out-of-scope ground applies.

finding.summary: isPrivateAddress omits IPv6 transition ranges that embed IPv4 (NAT64 64:ff9b::/96, 6to4 2002::/16, Teredo 2001::/32)
finding.evidence: `isPrivateAddress` handles dotted-quad IPv4, `::`/`::1`, IPv4-mapped/-compatible (`::ffff:*`), `fc00::/7` and `fe80::/10` (lines 131-148), but not the transition prefixes that carry an IPv4 address in later words. On a network with a NAT64 gateway (common on IPv6-only hosts and some CI runners), a `src` of `http://[64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe]/latest/meta-data/` is a literal, passes `ipLiteral`, is not matched by any rule (words[0]=0x0064 → first=0x00, not fc/fd, not fe80), is allowed, and reaches 169.254.169.254. `2002:7f00:1::` (6to4 → 127.0.0.1) is the same shape. Also unmatched on the IPv4 side: 198.18.0.0/15, 192.0.0.0/24, 224.0.0.0/4 and 255.255.255.255. Severity reflects the SSRF impact if the deployment has such a gateway; confidence is low because it depends on the host's network having NAT64/6to4 configured.

verdict.reason: The code matches the finding verbatim. isPrivateAddress (image-fetcher.ts:131-148) only recognizes IPv4-mapped/compatible forms when words[0..4] are all zero (line 137), plus fc00::/7 (line 145) and fe80::/10 (line 146); there is no handling of NAT64 64:ff9b::/96, 6to4 2002::/16, or Teredo 2001::/32. For 64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe, parseIPv6 returns [0x0064,0xff9b,0,0,0,0,0xa9fe,0xa9fe]: the zero-prefix branch is skipped, first=0x00 fails the fc/fd test, and words[0]&0xffc0=0x0040 fails the fe80 test, so it returns false. That value is reachable: assertFetchableImageUrl treats a bracketed host as a literal (ipLiteral, lines 76-81), skips the DNS path entirely, and returns/allows at line 193 when isPrivateAddress is false — so an attacker-controlled document src reaches 169.254.169.254 through a NAT64 gateway, with the response bytes embedded in the exported PDF/DOCX. The IPv4 side is likewise incomplete: isPrivateIPv4 (lines 83-90) omits 198.18.0.0/15, 192.0.0.0/24, 224.0.0.0/4 and 255.255.255.255. The existing tests (test/image-fetcher.test.ts:172-197) cover none of these, and no caller-side guard filters IPv6 literals before line 188. SSRF/unsafe input handling is in the Security lane; exploitability is network-conditional (needs NAT64/6to4), which lowers likelihood but is not a refutation ground.
